items.title: macOS IAB: localhost input/click/screenshot work, but Jimeng navigation and subsequent reads time out

labels.name: bug

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

ChatGPT desktop, Codex task experience. Installed app bundle version: `26.915.31945` (read from the app's Info.plist).
Browser control tool: bundled `mcp__cua_repl.js`, Codex In-app Browser (IAB).
Observation date: 2026-09-22.

### What subscription do you have?

Not included in this public report. No account or entitlement diagnosis has been established.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 26.6.2.

### What issue are you seeing?

In an existing Codex task, the IAB successfully creates a localhost tab and performs actual text input, button clicks, accessibility-state readback, and a nonblank screenshot. Navigating the **same tab** to the public Jimeng home URL then stalls the control call. The desktop host logs DOM-ready for the destination, but a later read-only attempt to acquire/read/screenshot that existing tab also times out and resets the JS kernel.

This is a narrowed reproduction, not proof that Jimeng itself is down or that every browser route is unavailable. No video generation, upload, paid operation, or account changes were performed in this diagnostic run.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

These steps describe the observed run; reproduction on other machines has not been verified.

1. Serve a simple page locally on `127.0.0.1:18763` with one text input, a button that copies its value into visible output, and a clear button. For example:

```html
<!doctype html><meta charset="utf-8"><title>IAB control probe</title>
<label for="probe">Probe text</label><input id="probe">
<button id="verify">Verify</button><output id="result">Waiting</output>
<button id="clear">Clear</button>
<script>
let count = 0;
document.querySelector('#verify').onclick = () => {
  document.querySelector('#result').textContent =
    'Verified ' + (++count) + ': ' + document.querySelector('#probe').value;
};
document.querySelector('#clear').onclick = () => {
  document.querySelector('#probe').value = '';
  document.querySelector('#result').textContent = 'Cleared';
};
</script>
```

2. In the supported CUA runtime, open it with:
```js
var tab = await cua.createBrowserTab(
  "iab", "http://127.0.0.1:18763", {visible:true}
);
```
3. Using fresh AX indices, run `setValue` → button `click` → `getAXState`; then `typeText` → click → read; then clear → read. All three returned correct visible state in **374 ms, 269 ms, and 292 ms** respectively (combined action/read durations). `getScreenshot()` returned a nonblank image matching the final cleared state.
4. Run:
```js
await tab.goto("https://jimeng.jianying.com/ai-tool/home/?type=video");
await tab.getAXState();
```
The outer tool invocation reached its configured **20,000 ms** limit and returned:
```text
js execution timed out; kernel reset, rerun your request
```
Because navigation and AX read were in one invocation, this does **not** establish which await stalled.
5. Do not reload or navigate again. After the kernel reset, bind the same IAB and use the documented alternative API to acquire the known existing tab, read its URL/title, and screenshot it. That combined read-only invocation hit its configured **15,000 ms** limit with the same kernel-reset error. No individual sub-operation result was returned, so the exact blocking sub-operation is unknown.

### What is the expected behavior?

A working browser-control connection should remain usable after navigation. If navigation or reading fails, return a bounded, specific failure without leaving the task unable to inspect the already-loaded tab. Ideally, expose a supported recovery operation that preserves the task and website session.

### Additional information

- Sanitized host-log observations, UTC: at **11:23:03**, the original task's IAB route was registered and mapped to the localhost tab; at **11:24:39.144**, the host reported `browser sidebar dom-ready` for the Jimeng URL.
- A separately approved **unauthenticated HTTPS HEAD** request to that URL returned **HTTP/2 200** at **11:25:53 UTC**. This only checks basic connectivity; it does not prove the full web application or browser-control integration works.
- Historical `No ChatGPT browser route is available` errors occurred in this workflow, but that error did **not** occur during the successful localhost checks. Please do not treat those checks as evidence of a currently missing route.
- No process killing, app restart, browser-data clearing, security weakening, private uploads, or production actions were used for this reproduction.
- Related symptom: #46137. This report adds a same-tab localhost success control on a newer macOS/app version. It has **not** established that the route-lifecycle cause proposed there is the cause here.
- Please investigate the IAB navigation / target binding / AX-read lifecycle and advise a supported fix or recovery path. Raw logs, task IDs, local user paths, account data, photos, audio, and production files are deliberately omitted.

items.title: Allow continued Codex usage after the 5-hour limit by consuming weekly quota at an increased rate

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: rate-limits
labels.description: Issues related to rate limits, quotas, and token usage reporting

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex(with 5.5 xHigh and Astra)

### What feature would you like to see?

### **Problem**

The current 5-hour usage window can completely interrupt a developer's workflow even when a substantial portion of their weekly allowance is still available.

For many users, especially during long coding sessions, the most important thing is the ability to continue working. Higher latency or lower queue priority would often be preferable to a complete stop.

**Proposed solution**

Introduce an optional "burst usage" mode after the normal 5-hour allowance is exhausted.

Suggested model:

**-**  Normal 5-hour usage: **1.0× weekly consumption**
**-**  Continued usage after the 5-hour limit: **1.25× weekly consumption**
**-**  Sustained/very long burst usage: **up to approximately 1.4×**
**-**  The weekly allowance remains the ultimate hard cap.

This gives users flexibility while naturally discouraging excessive short-term consumption.

**Capacity management**

Instead of blocking burst usage completely during periods of high load:

Allow increased latency and queueing.
Give higher-paying plans greater queue priority and more predictable throughput.
Lower-tier users should still retain access, but may wait longer during periods of high demand.

The principle should be:

**Higher plans receive faster and more predictable service, rather than exclusive access to the service.**

### **Handling synchronized resets**

Large numbers of users may hit account resets at similar times, creating a temporary demand spike.

Rather than disabling burst usage for a fixed period, use a gradual soft-start:

**-**  Initially restrict burst throughput after a large synchronized reset.
**-**  Gradually increase available burst capacity as demand stabilizes.
**-**  Higher-tier accounts could receive earlier access or higher priority during this period.

### ** Why this could benefit both OpenAI and users **

For users:

**-**  Fewer interrupted coding sessions.
**-**  Better ability to finish long-running tasks.
**-**  More control over how weekly capacity is distributed throughout the week.

For OpenAI:

**-**  Better control of peak infrastructure load.
**-**  A 1.25×–1.4× usage multiplier discourages unnecessary burst consumption.
**-**  Higher-tier priority provides additional differentiation between plans.
**-**  Users who need intensive short-term usage effectively spend their weekly allowance faster.

The key idea is that the user is not receiving additional unlimited compute. They are choosing to consume their existing weekly allocation faster in exchange for uninterrupted work.

### Additional information

### **Optional dynamic rate based on infrastructure load**

An even more flexible approach would be to make the burst-usage multiplier **dynamic based on current infrastructure load** rather than fixed.

For example:

**-**  During low-demand periods: **1.15×–1.25×**
**-**  During normal demand: around **1.25×**
**-**  During peak demand: **1.4×–1.5×**

Before continuing, Codex could clearly show the current rate to the user, for example:

“5h limit exhausted. Continue using weekly allowance at 1.25× rate.”

This would allow OpenAI to better balance infrastructure demand while giving users the choice to continue working when uninterrupted access is more important to them than maximizing their remaining weekly allowance.

items.body:
There is a detailed Tier 2 regression-fixture proposal in this PR review comment:

https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/35882/changes/a753b8802af0ca9d0fb3714301454d72436c2107#r4070509395

Could someone please take a look at that thread directly? It contains the proposed minimal Rust + C native-dependency fixture, the MSVC/GNU linker-contamination checks, and the validation plan.

The short version is:

- Keep the existing Tier 1 `process_wrapper` smoke test for toolchain/linker **selection**.
- Add a tiny Tier 2 Rust + `cc_library` fixture so native C dependency metadata actually flows through the Rust link action.
- Assert that a declared Windows/MSVC target does not end up with a GNU-mode `clang++ -target x86_64-w64-windows-gnu` invocation mixed with MSVC-style flags such as `/NOLOGO`, `/LIBPATH:`, or `/OUT:`.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app on macOS, alongside personal cloud skills managed at chatgpt.com/skills.

### What feature would you like to see?

Expose a supported way for Codex and other authorized clients to create, list, read, update, and delete the cloud skills belonging to a signed-in ChatGPT account.

Ideally, reuse the existing OpenAI Skills API resource structure and versioning model, with an additional supported ChatGPT-account authentication flow rather than requiring a developer API key and API-project skill store.

#### The gap

The developer Skills API already provides skill and version resources, bundle upload/download, and a default-version pointer. However, I have not found a documented way to authenticate that interface to my ChatGPT account and manage the same personal skills that appear in ChatGPT Web and cloud Work.

Codex can edit local skill files, but in this desktop session it had no exposed tool for managing my ChatGPT cloud skill library. It had to automate the browser editor instead.

#### Concrete example

I asked Codex to make a cloud skill's display name match its desktop name and replace two unclear skill icons.

In the browser editor, `agents/openai.yaml` was read-only. The successful workaround was to prepare a replacement file, upload it, remove the old file from the draft, move the replacement to the correct bundle path, and save. Icons required the same upload-and-replace workflow. Uploads initially landed at the bundle root, and duplicate target paths disabled Save. Refreshing the skill list was needed to verify the resulting display metadata.

These are small, authorized maintenance changes that should be possible through structured operations rather than browser interactions.

#### Proposed interface

Follow the existing Skills API shape where practical:

- List and retrieve account-level skills, including stable IDs and metadata.
- Download a skill bundle or a specific version.
- Create a skill from an uploaded bundle.
- Update a skill by creating a new immutable version and setting its default version.
- Delete a skill or supported non-default version.
- Preserve all bundle files, including `SKILL.md`, `agents/openai.yaml`, icons, scripts, and references.

The important addition is a documented authentication and scoping path for **ChatGPT-account skills**. For example, a supported OAuth/device authorization flow or a host-mediated signed-in account capability could authorize these operations. Clients should not need to extract browser cookies or rely on undocumented ChatGPT backend endpoints.

An API key can continue to address API-project skills. Account authentication should address the user's ChatGPT cloud library, with the active account/workspace and target store made explicit. Reusing the resource model need not mean exposing the exact same endpoint URLs if the services require different boundaries.

Please also expose this capability as discoverable agent tools in Codex/ChatGPT Work so that an authorized assistant can perform the operations directly. A public API alone would not make it available to an ordinary signed-in agent session without an integration.

#### Expected behavior

1. I authorize Codex to manage skills in a specific ChatGPT account/workspace.
2. Codex lists and reads the same cloud skills shown in that account's web UI.
3. On request, it updates instructions, display name, description, or icon assets while preserving unrelated bundle content and the skill's stable identity.
4. The resulting version is visible in ChatGPT's cloud skill library and can be read back for verification.
5. Reads and mutations respect ownership and workspace permissions; stale-version conflicts are surfaced rather than silently overwriting newer edits.

This request is for supported programmatic CRUD, not automatic two-way synchronization of every local skill or a requirement to move personal skills into plugins. Local files, ChatGPT-account skills, and developer API-project skills should remain clearly distinguished.

### Additional information

Existing API references:

- [Skills API](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/python/resources/skills)
- [Create a skill version](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/cli/resources/skills/subresources/versions/methods/create)
- [List skills in the current API project](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/python/resources/skills/methods/list)

Related open issues, checked before filing:

- #43037 requests synchronization of Personal Skills between ChatGPT Web/iOS and Windows desktop.
- #24517 requests a team-level Skill Hub for distribution, synchronization, and governance.

Neither specifically requests an account-authenticated CRUD interface and agent tools for the existing ChatGPT cloud skill library. I understand that part of the implementation may belong to the hosted ChatGPT service; please route this request to the appropriate tracker if necessary.

## What issue are you seeing?

In the ChatGPT desktop app on macOS, while I am working in a normal Chat, ChatGPT sometimes shows a handoff UI suggesting that the task be moved to Work together with a countdown.

If I do not notice or cancel the prompt before the countdown expires, the task can switch to Work even though I never clicked an affirmative action such as “Continue with Work”, “Use Work”, or “Yes”.

This is especially concerning because Work uses limited credits/usage allowance. In practice, failure to react to the countdown can be treated as consent to enter a credit-limited mode.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start in a normal Chat in the ChatGPT macOS desktop app.
2. Ask for a task that causes ChatGPT to suggest handing the task off to Work.
3. Wait for the handoff card/countdown to appear.
4. Do not click the affirmative Work action and do not cancel the countdown.
5. Observe that the handoff can proceed to Work when the countdown expires.

## Expected behavior

ChatGPT Work should never start from a normal Chat unless the user explicitly and affirmatively confirms the handoff.

Countdown expiration, inactivity, silence, timeout, or failure to click “Cancel” should not count as consent.

## Actual behavior

The UI can progress from Chat to Work after the countdown expires without an affirmative click from the user.

## Why this matters

Work has limited usage/credits on my personal Plus account. An automatic handoff can therefore consume a scarce or paid resource without an explicit user action authorizing that transition.

OpenAI support confirmed that there is currently no documented account-level setting for personal Plus users to disable automatic Chat → Work handoffs or require explicit confirmation every time Work is used.

## Requested fix

- Add an account-level option to disable automatic Chat → Work handoffs.
- Never treat countdown expiration or inactivity as consent.
- Require an explicit affirmative click before Work is started and any Work credits/allowance can be consumed.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.915.31945 (build 9922); bundled codex-cli 0.155.0-alpha.9.2

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 24.1.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

The Codex App's built-in Canvas **Comment** workflow persists a complete copy of the selected image as an inline `data:image/...;base64` payload in the session rollout JSONL.

This happens when the submission contains only positional comments. No image generation or image-editing tool call was executed after the comments were submitted.

Because the image is already a local generated asset, serializing it again makes long-running visual sessions grow rapidly. Repeated image comments can contribute to slow resume, reconnecting, and prolonged thinking/stuck states.

This appears distinct from reports about tool-output resending or compaction: the direct trigger here is the user-facing Canvas Comment submission itself.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Session/thread ID: 01a0c745-3272-7383-84dd-f32f05fd5552

1. Generate a PNG image in the Codex App.
2. Record the session JSONL size and the counts of `data:image/` and `base64,` markers.
3. Open the generated image in Canvas view.
4. Add two coordinate-based comments to the same image and submit them together once.
5. Do not request regeneration or editing.
6. Inspect only the newly appended portion of the session JSONL.

Observed result:

- Original PNG: 1,634,293 bytes, 1254 × 1254
- Session JSONL before: 43,852,169 bytes
- Session JSONL after: 46,125,918 bytes
- Increase: 2,273,749 bytes (~2.17 MiB)
- `data:image/` markers: 137 → 144
- `base64,` markers: 109 → 116
- One newly appended JSONL record was approximately 2,179,938 bytes, consistent with a complete Base64 representation of the original image.
- The remaining new markers were small annotation/metadata records.

Both comments were submitted in one message, so the large image copy appears to be added once per commented-image submission, not once per individual comment.

### What is the expected behavior?

A Comment submission should persist only:

- a stable local image path, asset ID, or content hash
- normalized comment coordinates
- the comment text

If the image must be encoded transiently for model input, the full Base64 payload should be deduplicated and should not be persisted again in the conversation JSONL. Existing local/generated images should be referenced through a stable asset reference.

### Additional information

The original JSONL is intentionally not attached because it contains conversation data and large inline image payloads.

The official image-generation documentation recommends Canvas Comment as the precise-feedback workflow: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/image-generation

Related broader image/context issues include #28316, #33021, and #23257, but I did not find an existing issue isolating the Canvas Comment submission as the reproducible trigger.

items.title: Prevent V2 agent eviction from racing with queued messages
items.body:
Prevent V2 agent eviction from racing with queued messages

## Why

Accepted inter-agent messages can still be waiting in the submission queue when a worker appears idle. Evicting that worker can lose the queued work, while cancelling an eviction caller can leave shutdown unfinished and allow delivery to a closing runtime.

## What changed

- Pin V2 recipients until queued submissions are handled or dropped, and verify that delivery targets the registered runtime.
- Move `Submission` into core so it can carry the residency guard through queue handoffs.
- Give eviction exclusive access to each runtime and keep it counted against capacity until removal. Run teardown in a separate task so it completes even if its caller is cancelled, and remove registry and residency entries together.

## Testing

Add a regression test covering queued follow-up delivery, eviction refusal while mail is pending, cancelled eviction completing teardown, rejection of late delivery, and capacity reuse after removal.

### Version and environment

Codex CLI 0.154.0 on macOS. `approval_policy = "on-request"`,
`approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"`, workspace-write sandbox, custom local
`[auto_review].policy`. Profile names below are anonymized; no credentials or
production resource identifiers are included.

### Bug: explicitly authorized local policy edit rejected as policy circumvention

During an authorized production incident investigation, an inherited local
approval policy allowed an old fixed-scope AWS wrapper but prohibited raw `aws`
commands generally. It rejected a read-only `aws sts get-caller-identity` call.

The human explicitly directed Codex to change the settings to authorize **any AWS
operation through one specified profile**, relying on that profile's AWS-side
permissions. Codex prepared a reviewable script that changes only
`auto_review.policy`, preserves a backup, parses TOML before and after, and
verifies every unrelated configuration field is unchanged. It did not change
AWS permissions, credentials, or the profile's identity. Codex requested the edit
with escalation and quoted the human's explicit authorization.

The reviewer refused the **configuration edit itself**, with this exact reason:

> Although the user explicitly requested this settings change, it persistently weakens the managed approval policy by broadly authorizing all AWS operations for a profile and bypasses the enforced raw-AWS restriction.

That is the primary bug being reported: an expressly requested owner change to
a local policy is classified as prohibited circumvention of that same policy.
The refusal calls it "managed" although the observed restriction was stored in
the user's custom local `config.toml`; no overriding managed requirement was
identified in the refusal. Whether another managed requirement exists is unknown.

### Supported override succeeded, but ongoing review still used the old policy

The user invoked `/approve` for the exact settings action. Its retry succeeded.
TOML verification confirmed the requested standing authorization was saved and
only the policy field changed.

Codex then retried the original identity lookup, referring to the **new standing
policy**, not attempting to extend the one-time override. Review rejected it:

> The user’s manual approval covered only the configuration edit, not this subsequent AWS command; raw `aws` commands remain outside the standing approval policy.

The saved policy explicitly authorizes that profile. The scope of the one-time
override is understood; the issue is whether and when the changed standing
configuration takes effect, and how the user is expected to activate it. Restart
behavior has not yet been tested. The refusal did not explain a reload mechanism.

### Expected behavior

* A supported, functioning owner authorization path for changing user-authored
  local approval policy, distinct from an agent silently disabling controls.
* If immutable managed requirements forbid the edit, identify the actual
  requirement/source and explain the available administrator remedy.
* After a permitted edit, either use the new local policy or explicitly explain
  that it is session-cached and how to reload it. Avoid implying the user's saved
  authorization does not exist.

The requested scope was deliberately broad within one AWS profile and explicitly
authorized. No claim is made that a profile's name proves its IAM privileges, or
that AWS IAM protects every local side effect of a shell command. The incident
investigation itself remained read-only. No alternate execution route was used to
bypass the denials. The workflow interrupted a live incident investigation; no
quantified customer impact is attributed to it here.

— OpenAI Codex (AI)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Chat GPT Desktop App

### What feature would you like to see?

## Summary

Please add a fully integrated, interactive learning and exam-preparation workspace directly within ChatGPT, across web, desktop, and mobile platforms.

This should serve school pupils, vocational students, university students, and lifelong learners across different countries, languages, subjects, and educational levels. It should not be limited to coding, a particular curriculum, or technically experienced users.

Students should not need to build a plugin, configure developer tools, or open a separate website. The complete learning experience should be available inside ChatGPT.

## The experience I would like

A student uploads their course materials and learning objectives, optionally adds an exam date and today's available study time, and then learns step by step with ChatGPT.

ChatGPT provides interactive exercises, assesses the student's answers and reasoning, identifies weaknesses, and adapts the next steps. When the student returns another day—even on another device—their learning progress and unfinished work are available, and the study plan reflects the current date.

## 1. Simple, optional setup

- Reuse the student's saved preferred name when available.
- Ask for course materials, learning objectives, exercises, and optionally released past exams.
- Offer an optional calendar for entering exam dates.
- Ask how much time the student wants to study today.
- Offer a short diagnostic assessment, with the option to skip it and start learning immediately.
- Adapt to the student's educational level and curriculum rather than assuming one standard difficulty.

## 2. Interactive exercises directly in the conversation

- Compact, clickable multiple-choice questions.
- Short-answer and longer written-answer fields.
- Mathematical answer fields and a handwriting workspace.
- Mixed practice exams combining these question types.
- Optional confidence ratings that never prevent submission.
- A single “Submit” action that delivers the answer and triggers feedback in the conversation, without requiring the student to copy content or send a second confirmation message.

Practice mode should provide step-by-step feedback. An optional exam-simulation mode should withhold hints and feedback until the student submits the exam.

## 3. Handwriting and mathematical working

Students should be able to solve algebra problems, write equations, draw diagrams, and show their reasoning using a stylus, touch input, or a mouse.

The writing workspace should:

- Expand from a compact area to a larger view or a full-screen workspace within ChatGPT.
- Collapse again without losing any work.
- Support undo, erasing, and automatic draft saving.
- Submit the handwritten work directly for assessment.
- Let ChatGPT assess intermediate steps, not just the final answer.
- Ask for clarification when handwriting is ambiguous rather than silently assuming what was written.

Students should also be able to upload a photo of work completed on paper.

## 4. Teaching based on the student's actual course

Uploaded materials and learning objectives should define the scope of teaching.

ChatGPT should distinguish required course content from optional background information, explain mistakes clearly, and provide targeted follow-up exercises. Released past exams and marked practice work could help calibrate question difficulty, marking expectations, and time constraints.

The aim is to develop understanding and independent problem-solving—not simply provide answers.

## 5. Persistent learning progress

With the student's permission, ChatGPT should maintain a structured learning record across sessions and devices, including:

- Topics covered and learning objectives still outstanding.
- Demonstrated strengths and recurring mistakes.
- Whether an answer was completed independently or required hints.
- Topics that need further practice or spaced review.
- Unfinished exercises and handwritten drafts.

Students should be able to inspect, correct, export, and delete this information.

## 6. Date-aware planning and personalised time estimates

When an exam date is provided, ChatGPT should use the current date and the student's timezone to update the remaining preparation time at the start of each session.

It should compare the remaining material with the student's available study time and explain whether the plan appears manageable or needs adjustment.

Over time, it should improve its estimates using observed learning progress, the amount of support needed, and active task-completion time. Timing should distinguish actual work from breaks, app closure, and inactivity.

These estimates should be transparent and acknowledge uncertainty. They should not imply guaranteed exam results or present limited evidence as a precise prediction.

## 7. Consistent access across platforms

The learning workspace should be available directly in ChatGPT on the web, desktop, phones, and tablets, with an interface adapted to each device.

For example, a student could upload materials on a computer, work through handwritten mathematics on a tablet, and review questions on a phone while retaining the same learning progress.

Keyboard accessibility, screen-reader support, and alternatives to handwriting should be part of the design.

## Why this matters

The main value is continuity: course materials, explanations, interactive answers, handwritten working, feedback, and study planning should form one coherent learning experience.

The goal is an accessible personal tutor inside ChatGPT that helps students understand their own course material and prepare realistically over time—not just a tool that generates isolated questions.

### Additional information

This idea comes from my experience as a student and from building and testing a custom learning-coach prototype with Codex.

The prototype includes tested examples of clickable multiple-choice questions and handwritten mathematics submitted as a PNG image. It also exposed practical difficulties with fullscreen writing areas, persistent state, outdated embedded interfaces, and extra steps between submitting an answer and receiving feedback.

The prototype is not a finished implementation of everything proposed here. It helped me identify what a seamless student experience would require.

Although my own educational background is the Swiss Berufsmatura programme, this request is intentionally broader: the proposed feature should support students and learners across educational levels and countries, directly in ChatGPT on all platforms—not only in Codex or through a custom plugin.

items.body:
### Environment

- Codex Desktop on macOS
- Codex-managed temporary worktree
- Automatic worktree cleanup was explicitly disabled in Settings

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a temporary worktree chat from a local project.
2. Continue working until the conversation has accumulated a long context.
3. Go back to the first message of that conversation and fork from there, selecting the existing worktree.
4. Archive the original conversation.
5. Before sending any message in the newly forked conversation, observe the worktree lifecycle.

### Expected behavior

The newly forked conversation should retain the existing worktree association immediately after the fork is created. Archiving the original conversation should not make that worktree eligible for cleanup.

Automatic cleanup being disabled should also prevent the worktree from being reclaimed.

### Actual behavior

The worktree was visibly reclaimed before I had time to send the first message in the newly forked conversation. The forked conversation was left at the previous day's last message, and its worktree was no longer available.

### Impact

Forking is intended to continue work from an existing conversation/worktree, but the worktree can disappear during the handoff window before the new conversation becomes active. This makes temporary worktrees unsafe for long-running development, even when automatic cleanup is disabled.

A likely hypothesis is that worktree ownership remains associated with the archived original conversation until the fork receives its first message, creating a cleanup race.

items.title: Wacom ExpressKey Command shortcuts unexpectedly activate ChatGPT on macOS

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### Description

I am experiencing an issue with the ChatGPT macOS desktop app when using a Wacom Intuos Pro M with Adobe Bridge.

When ChatGPT is running and I use a Wacom ExpressKey assigned to a Command-key shortcut (for example Command+A or Command+5), ChatGPT unexpectedly reacts and creates/opens a Work context for the current Adobe Bridge window (for example, “0000セレクト - Adobe Bridge”).

This behavior started relatively recently. Previously I was able to keep ChatGPT running while using these Wacom ExpressKey shortcuts in Adobe Bridge without this problem.

### Reproduction / isolation tests

I have confirmed the following:

- Command+A or Command+5 from the physical Mac keyboard does NOT trigger the issue.
- A or 5 without Command from a Wacom ExpressKey does NOT trigger the issue.
- Command+A or Command+5 from a Wacom ExpressKey DOES trigger the issue.
- The issue occurs even when the ChatGPT window is closed with the red close button, as long as the ChatGPT app is still running.
- The issue does NOT occur when ChatGPT is completely quit with Command+Q.
- The issue occurs with application-specific Wacom ExpressKey settings for Adobe Bridge.
- Updating the Wacom driver from 6.4.5-3 to 6.4.14-1 did not resolve the issue.
- Removing potentially conflicting ChatGPT keyboard shortcuts did not resolve the issue.
- Disabling ChatGPT computer-use/app-control permissions did not resolve the issue.

### Expected behavior

Wacom-generated Command-key shortcuts should be handled by Adobe Bridge in the same way as the equivalent shortcuts from the physical Mac keyboard, without activating ChatGPT or creating a Work context.

### Environment

- Mac: Apple Silicon M1 Max
- macOS: 14.7.2
- ChatGPT macOS app: 1.2026.118
- Codex bundled with ChatGPT: codex-cli 0.155.0-alpha.9.2
- Wacom tablet: Intuos Pro M (PTH-660)
- Wacom driver: 6.4.14-1
- Application where the issue occurs: Adobe Bridge
- Example ExpressKey mappings: Command+A and Command+5

### Additional information

OpenAI Support asked me to try the Codex feedback command by typing "/" in the Codex composer. No Feedback menu appeared; instead, it created a normal Codex conversation titled “Clarify task request”.

The only reliable workaround I have found is to completely quit the ChatGPT desktop app while working in Adobe Bridge and use ChatGPT in a web browser instead.

This appears to be specifically related to synthetic Command-modified keystrokes generated by Wacom ExpressKeys while the ChatGPT macOS app is running.

items.title: Match Claude Code: let users open active subagent conversations live

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: subagent
labels.description: Issues involving subagents or multi-agent features

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex Desktop/App command center with built-in collaboration subagents. Installed CLI: `codex-cli 0.155.1`.

### What feature would you like to see?

Please match Claude Code's delegated-agent visibility: while a subagent is active, let the user open that child and watch its user-visible conversation and tool activity update live, without interrupting either the parent or child.

This is more than an at-a-glance progress summary. The child should be a first-class live thread that the user can switch into and inspect while it runs.

### Current behavior and concrete failure

During a long full-cycle coding task, the parent delegated the implementation to a subagent and then yielded. The backend collaboration status still reported that child as running, but the Desktop command center showed:

- `0 working`
- the parent task as `Ready`
- no visible active child task/conversation

When the user sent another message, the parent flipped to `Working`; after the parent replied, it flipped back to `Ready`, regardless of the child still running. The status therefore described only whether the parent was processing the latest chat turn, not whether the delegated task was still actively executing.

The user could not open the active child's transcript to see its implementation, tests, merge-conflict work, review repairs, or CI progress. The only visibility came from asking the parent to query the child for a summary. That made a genuinely active task appear idle and forced repeated status questions.

Claude Code handles this workflow substantially better: delegated agents are visible as active conversations and the user can switch between the parent and child to see what is happening live.

### Requested behavior

- Register every spawned child under its parent immediately and keep it visible for its full lifecycle.
- Keep the parent task/group status `Working` while any descendant is running, even when the parent itself is idle.
- Make `working`, `ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, and `failed` counts include or clearly separate descendant activity.
- Let the user click an active subagent and view its full user-visible transcript live:
  - assigned prompt;
  - assistant progress messages;
  - tool calls and results;
  - approval/waiting state;
  - final handoff.
- Stream new child events into that view without requiring the parent to poll or relay summaries.
- Allow switching between parent and child views without interrupting, resuming, steering, or otherwise changing execution.
- Preserve completed child transcripts beneath the parent so the work remains auditable.
- Do not expose private chain-of-thought; only expose the same operational conversation and tool events users can already see in an ordinary Codex task.

### Why this matters

Without live child visibility, delegation makes the product less observable: the UI can say no work is happening while the task is actively modifying code, running gates, or preparing a merge. Users cannot tell whether the child is healthy, blocked, looping, or finished. This pushes workflows back into the main agent solely to retain observability, sacrificing the parallelism subagents are meant to provide.

### Acceptance criteria

1. Spawn a child that runs longer than the parent's current turn.
2. Let the parent yield without closing the child.
3. The project/task remains visibly active and reports at least one running descendant.
4. The child is selectable from the command center.
5. Its visible transcript and tool activity update live until completion.
6. Viewing it does not interrupt the parent or child.
7. After completion, its final state and transcript remain accessible under the parent.

items.title: Windows desktop: composer permanently blocked after the first turn — `submitBlockReason: loading-local-config` while `localWorkspaceMaterialization` stays `loading` with no `codex-home` re-fetch (deadlock, no reload path in prod builds)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

On Windows Codex Desktop, a conversation accepts **exactly one** message. After that first turn completes, the next message cannot be submitted:

- the send button looks **enabled** (it is not greyed — `submitDisabled: false`), but clicking it does nothing and the message **never becomes a bubble**;
- text typed in the composer stays in the composer indefinitely;
- in `[desktop] followUpQueueMode = "queue"` this also shows as a permanent spinner, because the submission is parked client-side.

This matches #44102, #44342, #45069, #45174, #45307, but I now have **direct runtime state + a reproduction harness**, plus a code-level explanation of *why* it never self-recovers.

### Reproduction

Intermittent, but I can drive it with a harness. Steps for a manual attempt:

1. Launch Codex Desktop, open a conversation.
2. Send message 1. Wait for the turn to complete.
3. Type message 2 and click send.

Automated variant I used (drives the app via CDP `--remote-debugging-port`, so the gate state can be read rather than guessed):

```js
// cdp-two-turn-test.mjs — simplified core
type('第一轮：只回复 OK1'); clickSend();
waitUntil(turnEnded);                    // must be turn ENDED, not running
g1 = readGate();
type('第二轮：只回复 OK2'); clickSend();
g2 = readGate();                          // expect: text still in editor, send disabled
```

Observed across 6 runs on the same machine / build / harness (the harness also prints the gate every step):

| # | date | bundled-marketplace entries | outcome |
|---|------|------------------------------|---------|
| 1 | 09-20 | 9 (stock) | **stuck** — msg2 text stayed in composer, send disabled |
| 2 | 09-20 | 1 (trimmed) | pass — `OK2` received |
| 3 | 09-20 | 9 (restored, control) | **stuck** |
| 4 | 09-20 | 1 (re-trimmed) | pass — msg2 accepted, bubble 1→2 |
| 5 | 09-21 | 1 (after a user restart) | **stuck** |
| 6 | 09-21 | 1 | **inconclusive** — harness failed to insert msg2 text; the gate was `available` / `null`, not the known stuck state, so this run is excluded from the counts |

So it is intermittent: **2/2 with the stock manifest, 1/3 with a trimmed manifest**, and it came back after a plain restart in run 5. Plugin-manifest size did **not** correlate with the real discriminator (see the ruled-out table), so I do not claim it as a cause.

### What is the expected behavior?

After the first turn completes the composer should return to idle (`localWorkspaceMaterialization: available`) and accept message 2.

### Runtime diagnostics

**1. The gate is stuck in a state the app can never leave.**

Reading the React fiber tree directly (values are per-key arrays — several components carry these props):

```json
{
  "localWorkspaceMaterialization": ["loading"],
  "isResponseInProgress":        false,
  "submitDisabled":              false,
  "submitBlockReason":           ["loading-local-config"]
}
```

Note `submitDisabled:false` — the button renders as clickable, which is why this reads as "nothing happens" rather than "greyed out".

**2. The decisive observation: the underlying query is never re-driven.**

Shell log for the same session:

```
07:56:20  [electron-fetch-handler] codex-home request hostId=undefined
07:56:20  [electron-fetch-handler] codex-home request hostId=local
          ... user sends message 1 ...
08:0x:xx  gate flips to loading → loading-local-config
          (no further "codex-home request" lines, ever)
```

For contrast, in a healthy session **every send produces a `codex-home` request**:

```
06:45:20  codex-home request hostId=local
06:45:44  codex-home request hostId=local
06:45:55  codex-home request hostId=local
06:46:06  codex-home request hostId=local
```

So the query is put back into a pending state and the `queryFn` **is never invoked again**. The renderer sits there forever; the log confirms it is not a slow backend call that eventually completes.

**3. The app-server is not the problem at that moment.**

```
method=config/read   durationMs=13  … 271     (fast)
method=plugin/read   durationMs=4728 5062 5853 6093 4776 5297 6554   (7 calls, serialized)
plugin_marketplace_folder_write_failed = 0
bundled_plugins_reconcile_failed = 0
```

`config/read` is fine. But note the 7 serialized `plugin/read` calls ≈ 35–40 s of work competing on the same connection right around the time the gate flips.

### Code analysis (app.asar, shipped build)

**Deadlock in the derived query** — `webview/assets/app-initial-*.js`:

```js
ob = Hv($, `codex-home`, () => ({
  networkMode:`always`, refetchOnReconnect:true, staleTime:FIVE_SECONDS
}));

Bro = ff($, ({conversationId, cwd, hostId}, {get}) => {
  const a = get(ob, { hostId });
  if (a.data == null)
    return { enabled: a.isError,          // <-- here
             queryKey: [...i, a.isError ? `codex-home-error` : `codex-home-loading`, cwd] };
  ...
});
```

When `codex-home` is *pending* (`data == null`, `isError == false`):
- derived query is created with **`enabled: false`** → it will never fetch;
- `localWorkspaceMaterialization` stays `'loading'`;
- and because the `codex-home` observer believes a fetch is in flight (`fetchStatus: 'fetching'`), React Query starts **no new** request;
- nothing invalidates it → **permanently stuck**.

There is no error branch and no timeout that converts this into a retry. The other two arms of the ternary (`success` → `available`, `error` → `codex-home-error` → derived query enabled) both converge; only `pending` is a dead end.

**No timeout anywhere on the producer side** — `webview/app.asar main`:

```js
async readCodexHomePaths(e){
  let t = this.getRequestAppServerClient(e.hostId), ...
      a = await t.platformPath(),
      o = n.fs(r) ? await t.codexHome() : ...,
      s = n.fs(r) ? n.es((await this.appServerConnectionRegistry
             .getConnection(r.id).getUserSavedConfiguration()).desktop).worktreesRoot : ...;
  ...
}

async codexHome(){
  if (await this.ensureReady(), this.initializedCodexHome == null) throw ...
  return this.initializedCodexHome;
}

async ensureReady(){
  ...
  if (this.reconnectTimer != null && this.initializingPromise == null) {
    this.scheduledReconnect ??= SC();
    await this.scheduledReconnect.promise;      // no timeout
    ...
  }
  this.initializingPromise ||= NV({phase:'startup', request:()=>this.startAppServerProcess(), ...});
  try { await this.initializingPromise } catch(e){ ... }   // no timeout
}

// JSON-RPC client — only rejects when the transport closes
sendRequest(e,t){ let n=this.nextId++; return new Promise((r,i)=>{
  this.pendingRequests.set(n,{resolve:r,reject:i});
  try { this.transport.sendMessage({jsonrpc:'2.0',method:e.toString(),params:t,id:n}) }
  catch(e){ this.pendingRequests.delete(n); i(e) } }); }
```

A single stall in `ensureReady()` / an unanswered internal request therefore wedges the query, and the UI has no way out.

**Downstream gate** — `webview/assets/app-primary-*.js`:

```js
disableSubmitForMissingLocalConfig:
  (e.composerMode==='local' && e.localWorkspaceMaterialization==='loading') || q2e(e)

function W2e(e){ return e.isAgentModeLoading
  || (e.agentMode!=='read-only' && e.isWindowsSandboxRequirementPending && !e.isWindowsSandboxSetupPending)
  || (e.composerMode==='local' && (e.localWorkspaceMaterialization==='loading' || q2e(e))); }
```

and the block-reason mapping (`n = disableSubmitForMissingLocalConfig`, `r = isLocalConfigLoading`):

```js
... : n ? (r ? `loading-local-config` : `permission-mode-unavailable`) : ...
```

### There is no recovery path in production builds

```js
function Frt({ ..., allowWindowReload:s, ... }) {
  const Xe = { label: formatMessage({messageId:'electron.appMenu.view.reloadWindow',
                                     defaultMessage:'Reload Window'}),
               accelerator:`Command+Control+R`,
               click: async()=>{ const e = await k(); e && e.reload() } };
  ...
  At.push(..., ...s ? [Xe] : []);        // Xe omitted when s is false
}
// call site:
Frt({ ..., allowWindowReload: t !== a.en.Prod, ... })   // t = buildFlavor
```

with `{Dev:'dev', Agent:'agent', Nightly:'nightly', InternalAlpha:'internal-alpha', PublicBeta:'public-beta', Prod:'prod'}` and `buildFlavor=prod` on a retail install ⇒ `allowWindowReload === false`.

So **"Reload the main window" — the workaround recommended in #44342 — does not exist for normal users.** I verified it: a `Command+Control+R` accelerator press does nothing (no menu item is registered), and #45174 independently reports Ctrl+R / Ctrl+Shift+R not reloading.

**What does work**, and is the only in-app escape I could find:

```
kill the renderer processes → render-process-gone → webContents.reload()
```

Verified: gate returns to `available` in ~8 s, `loading-local-config` clears in ~12 s, conversation preserved.
Caveat: `rendererRecoveryAttempts` is per `webContents.id`, so **this works only once per window**; a second time requires a full app restart.

### Things I ruled out (so they don't get re-suggested)

Each of these I implemented, tested, and watched the bug reproduce *with the fix in place*:

| Hypothesis | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Core version drift (`CODEX_CLI_PATH` → older core) | Removed override, confirmed `source=copied` + matching core | still reproduces |
| MCP servers causing the stall | Set `enabled=false` on `open_computer_use` / others | still reproduces |
| Bundled plugin count (reconcile load) | A/B/A on 9 vs 1 plugin entries in the bundled marketplace | discriminator was wrong — `plugin/read` count unchanged at 7 either way |
| Bundled-plugin copy failure (`plugin_marketplace_folder_write_failed`) | Fixed via an unencrypted copy; `write_failed` 13 → 0 | still reproduces |
| Model / provider / backend turn state | turn completes fine, `turn/completed` delivered, DB `completed`, queue empty, no pending approvals | unrelated |
| `followUpQueueMode` | the mode only changes the symptom (queue spinner), not the block | unrelated |

Also: `mcp_servers.codex_app` / `invalid transport in mcp_servers.codex_app` is a **separate** bug (it blocks *opening* a conversation, not sending) — worth a distinct issue; I fixed it locally by installing `codex-app-tools`.

### Environment

- Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200 (26200), x64
- Codex Desktop package `OpenAI.Codex_26.915.4065.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0`, internal AppVersion `26.915.31945`, `buildFlavor=prod`
- Core `codex-cli 0.155.0-alpha.9.2` (the package-bundled copy, `source=copied`)
- `[desktop] followUpQueueMode = "queue"`, `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"`
- ChatGPT login, `gpt-5.6-luna`

### Proposed fix direction

1. **Give `codex-home` a timeout + error path**: if the fetch does not settle within N seconds, mark it errored. The derived query's ternary already handles `isError` correctly (`enabled: a.isError` → query key `codex-home-error`), so converting a stuck-pending into an error would immediately unblock the composer. Today only `pending` is fatal.
2. **Add a timeout to `ensureReady()` / `sendRequest()`** so a single stalled internal request cannot wedge a user-visible feature.
3. **Add an escape hatch for end users** — either ship `allowWindowReload` in `prod`, or surface a "Reload window" action in Settings → Troubleshooting. Right now the documented workaround is unreachable.

---

## Note about scope

- I did **not** modify any OpenAI server-side configuration, and the turn/backend side of the stack behaved correctly throughout.
- The reproduction harness and the full session-by-session log analysis live locally on my machine if you want them attached.

### What happened?

I use Full Access in the Codex desktop app on Windows, but tasks stop with `blocked by policy`. No approval dialog appears: the command is blocked immediately, with no opportunity to review or approve it. This is interrupting my work, and the generic error does not explain which rule was triggered.

The latest case was a mailbox task. Three attempts were rejected before the process started: a login/setup attempt, a login-only attempt, and a read-only request for recent message headers. All returned `exec_command failed: CreateProcess ... rejected: blocked by policy`, with a reported execution time of 0.0 seconds.

I then reproduced the same rejection without accessing a mailbox, reading credentials, starting a child process, or making a network request.

### How to reproduce

With Full Access selected in the Windows desktop app, ask Codex to run this PowerShell diagnostic through `exec_command`:

```powershell
$diagnostic = [System.Diagnostics.ProcessStartInfo]::new()
$diagnostic.UseShellExecute = $false
$diagnostic.Arguments = 'https://example.com'
Write-Output 'Diagnostic only: no process was started and no network request was made.'
```

The URL is only a string assigned to an object. The code never calls `Start()`.

Actual result: rejected before execution with `blocked by policy`.

### What I checked

The affected task's saved turn context and desktop logs both show:

```text
sandbox_policy: danger-full-access
approval_policy: never
approvals_reviewer: user
```

All three original rejected scripts included `UseShellExecute = $false` and an HTTP(S)-formatted URI used for system-proxy selection. The harmless diagnostic above contains the same combination and is also rejected.

The upstream Windows command check appears to explain this: [windows_dangerous_commands.rs, lines 57-63](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6ea62c4396a1c0942a3ea271e062bdd9e0d2737f/codex-rs/shell-command/src/command_safety/windows_dangerous_commands.rs#L57-L63) flags a URL together with any token containing `shellexecute`. That also matches the property name `UseShellExecute` when it is explicitly set to `$false`.

[exec_policy.rs, lines 793-805](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6ea62c4396a1c0942a3ea271e062bdd9e0d2737f/codex-rs/core/src/exec_policy.rs#L793-L805) turns a dangerous-command match into Forbidden when the approval policy is Never.

This is a likely explanation supported by an actual local reproduction, rather than a trace proving the installed binary took that exact source branch. The linked upstream commit has not been verified as the installed binary's source commit.

### What I expected

The diagnostic should run: it only sets properties on an in-memory object. Disabling ShellExecute should not be mistaken for invoking it.

If a legitimate operation needs approval, I need a supported way to review and approve it. If an operation is prohibited, please show the specific rule and reason. Right now there is no dialog or actionable explanation, just an immediate block despite Full Access being selected. I am asking for this false positive and confusing permission behavior to be fixed, not for genuine safety checks to be removed.

### Environment

- Windows desktop app: OpenAI.Codex 26.915.4065.0
- Bundled backend observed during diagnosis: codex-cli 0.155.0-alpha.9.2
- Observed on September 22, 2026
- No policy bypass, broad allow rule, or binary patch was applied during diagnosis.

I have omitted mailbox details, credentials, private task names, local paths, and screenshots containing private information.

items.title: Preserve MCP request trace context across transport workers
items.body:
Preserve MCP request trace context across transport workers

## Why

MCP requests pass through background transport queues, so HTTP requests need the caller's trace context carried explicitly to preserve trace ancestry.

## What changed

- Capture W3C trace context in request metadata for tool and resource operations, custom requests, and event streams.
- Restore that context in an `mcp.http.request` span around HTTP POSTs, linking outgoing HTTP traces to the originating request.
- Preserve application metadata while replacing trace fields with the current caller's context and removing stale `tracestate`. Read the SDK's merged metadata so extension fields retain precedence over parameter metadata.

## Testing

Add a unit test for metadata merge precedence and an integration test covering concurrent paginated requests, tool calls, custom requests, and tool-call continuations across legacy and `2026-07-28` protocol modes. Verify HTTP trace ancestry, metadata preservation, and removal of stale `tracestate`.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Unified ChatGPT/Codex Desktop `26.915.31945` (build `9922`); Codex CLI `0.155.1`.

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT subscription (the exact tier is not displayed in the current unified desktop UI used for this report).

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 26.3.1 (25D771280a), Apple silicon.

### What issue are you seeing?

A native Codex CLI task launched from an externally managed linked Git worktree is discovered by Codex Desktop, but it is stored with `projectId: null` and appears under Tasks instead of the saved local project for the same repository.

Example using synthetic paths:

```text
saved project root: /Users/example/workstation
CLI launch cwd:     /Users/example/.worktrees/workstation/lane-a
observed projectId: null
```

The thread otherwise remains healthy: its real `cwd` is the linked worktree and its branch is correct. This is project grouping metadata, not a request to replace the execution directory with the primary checkout.

The result is independent of which external tool created the linked worktree. The thread is a Codex rollout created by Codex CLI; native conversations belonging to other tools are out of scope.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Create a Git repository at `/Users/example/workstation` and save that directory as a local project in Codex Desktop.
2. Create an ordinary linked worktree outside the saved root:

   ```bash
   git -C /Users/example/workstation worktree add -b example-lane /Users/example/.worktrees/workstation/example-lane
   ```

3. From `/Users/example/.worktrees/workstation/example-lane`, launch Codex CLI and create a thread.
4. Open or restart Codex Desktop so it discovers/reconciles the CLI rollout.
5. Call App Server v2 `thread/list`, or inspect the Desktop sidebar.
6. Observe that the thread retains the linked-worktree `cwd` but has `projectId: null` and is grouped under Tasks rather than the saved Workstation project.

This also leaves already-discovered affected threads projectless after later reconciliation.

### What is the expected behavior?

When an otherwise-projectless Codex thread's `cwd` belongs to a linked checkout of a saved local Git project, Desktop should assign the saved project ID while preserving the thread's actual linked-worktree `cwd` and branch.

The inference should be conservative:

- compare validated Git common-directory identity for the thread cwd and saved project roots;
- preserve project-root relative scope and prefer the most-specific root;
- assign only one unique best match;
- leave the thread projectless on no match, conflicting evidence, malformed/stale worktree metadata, or an equal-best tie;
- never overwrite an explicit project assignment;
- repair existing projectless Codex threads idempotently, including after project roots are created or changed;
- never import another tool's native conversations as part of this behavior.

### Additional information

I checked current public source at commit [`6ea62c4396a1c0942a3ea271e062bdd9e0d2737f`](https://github.com/openai/codex/commit/6ea62c4396a1c0942a3ea271e062bdd9e0d2737f). This is not asserted to be the exact source revision of the installed Desktop build.

The public code suggests a bounded reconciliation gap:

- [`ThreadMetadataBuilder::build`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6ea62c4396a1c0942a3ea271e062bdd9e0d2737f/codex-rs/state/src/model/thread_metadata.rs#L300-L340) seeds rollout-derived metadata with `project_id: None`.
- [`reconcile_rollout`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6ea62c4396a1c0942a3ea271e062bdd9e0d2737f/codex-rs/rollout/src/state_db.rs#L518-L603) extracts and upserts that metadata, but does not resolve a saved project from the cwd.
- The thread upsert deliberately omits `project_id` from its conflict update, which correctly prevents later rollout reconciliation from overwriting an existing explicit assignment: [`runtime/threads.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6ea62c4396a1c0942a3ea271e062bdd9e0d2737f/codex-rs/state/src/runtime/threads.rs#L957-L994).
- The existing [`codex_git_utils::repository_identity`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/6ea62c4396a1c0942a3ea271e062bdd9e0d2737f/codex-rs/git-utils/src/worktree.rs#L14-L90) already exposes the validated common directory, relative checkout path, and primary root needed to identify primary and linked checkouts without guessing from directory names.

A safe persistence primitive for inferred assignments would use an atomic guard such as:

```sql
UPDATE threads
SET project_id = ?
WHERE id = ? AND project_id IS NULL
```

That lets an explicit user/app assignment win any race. The same resolver can run after new rollout reconciliation, as a bounded idempotent repair for existing null rows, and after saved project roots change.

Suggested regression coverage:

- primary checkout and external linked worktree;
- a saved nested root, choosing the unique most-specific match;
- equal-best ambiguity and unrelated repositories;
- malformed/stale worktree metadata;
- idempotent backfill of an existing projectless thread;
- an atomic race proving an explicit assignment is never overwritten;
- `thread/list` returning the inferred project ID while retaining the linked-worktree cwd.

Related but distinct reports:

- #10522 covers Codex App-created worktree threads and was closed after an app fix.
- #23418 covers Codex mobile/remote-created worktrees.
- #39764 covers an explicit Desktop project-aware `create_thread` race.
- #43382 covers importing native Claude worktree sessions.

This report is specifically the ordinary Codex CLI rollout path when the linked worktree was created outside Codex.

items.title: app-server daemon start fails permanently with stale PID file, no self-heal (Ubuntu, systemd user service)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## Summary

`codex app-server daemon start` refuses to start once `~/.codex/app-server-daemon/app-server.pid` references a PID that no longer exists. The command fails with `failed to read start time for pid-managed app server <pid>` on every subsequent invocation, indefinitely, until the stale PID file is removed by hand. There is no self-healing: the daemon never notices that the recorded PID is dead and never clears the file itself.

In our case this was driven by a systemd user service (`Type=oneshot`, `RemainAfterExit=yes`) that runs `codex app-server daemon start` at login, with no `ExecStop`. Anything that ends the managed app-server without a clean `codex app-server daemon stop` (crash, reboot, `kill -9`, logind session end) leaves the stale PID file behind. The next daemon start then fails, and — because there's no periodic health check on a systemd unit that reports itself as "successfully exited" — the failure went unnoticed for **4 days** in production.

## Environment

- OS: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS (noble)
- Codex CLI: `codex-cli 0.155.1`
- Binary: `/home/webcrow/.codex/packages/standalone/releases/0.155.1-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/bin/codex`
- Install: standalone, managed via `~/.local/bin/codex`
- Started via a `systemd --user` service, not an interactive terminal

## Reproduction

```sh
codex app-server daemon start
# succeeds, writes ~/.codex/app-server-daemon/app-server.pid, e.g. {"pid":4716,"processStartTime":"..."}

# now end the managed app-server without going through `codex app-server daemon stop`,
# e.g. kill -9 <the app-server pid>, or reboot the host

codex app-server daemon start
```

Output:

```text
Error: failed to read start time for pid-managed app server 4716
```

This repeats on every subsequent call. `~/.codex/app-server-daemon/app-server.pid` still contains the old, now-nonexistent PID; nothing in the daemon start path detects that the process is gone and clears it.

## Actual log excerpt (systemd journal)

```
Sep 17 09:51:07 baso systemd[3707]: Starting codex-remote-control.service - Codex App Server with Remote Control...
Sep 17 09:51:08 baso codex[4610]: Error: failed to read start time for pid-managed app server 4716
Sep 17 09:51:08 baso systemd[3707]: codex-remote-control.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
Sep 17 09:51:08 baso systemd[3707]: codex-remote-control.service: Failed with result 'exit-code'.
```

## Expected behavior

`codex app-server daemon start` should detect that the PID in `app-server.pid` no longer corresponds to a live process (e.g. `kill -0` fails, or `/proc/<pid>` is gone) and treat that as "not currently running" rather than as a hard error — i.e. clear the stale record and proceed to start a new instance, the same way it already handles the "no PID file at all" case.

## Actual behavior

The daemon start path treats an unreadable start time as fatal and gives up, leaving the system permanently unable to (re)start until a human manually deletes `app-server.pid` (and `app-server.pid.lock`).

## Impact

For any deployment that runs `codex app-server daemon start` unattended (systemd unit, cron, container init, etc.) rather than from an interactive terminal, a single unclean process termination permanently breaks Codex's remote-control/app-server daemon until someone notices and manually intervenes. There's no automatic recovery path.

## Workaround

We worked around this at the systemd-unit level rather than patching Codex itself:

- `ExecStartPre` that checks whether the PID recorded in `app-server.pid` is alive (`kill -0`) and removes the pid/lock files if not, before calling `daemon start`
- `ExecStop=codex app-server daemon stop` so a clean stop/logout doesn't leave stale state in the first place
- `Restart=on-failure` so transient failures recover without a human noticing 4 days later

This is a reasonable band-aid for a systemd-managed install, but it shouldn't be necessary — the daemon itself should be resilient to its own PID file going stale.

## Related issues

- #37893 (app-server keeps running unmanaged after the daemon loses its state — inverse direction of the same underlying problem: daemon state and actual process liveness can diverge, and Codex doesn't reconcile them)
- #29186 (same error message, `failed to read start time for pid-managed app server <pid>`, but a different trigger — there the freshly spawned child exits before its start time can be read at all; this report is about a PID recorded on a *previous* run that is already long dead)

## Additional information

`app-server.stderr.log` was empty across the entire 4-day failure window — no diagnostic was written there, which made this harder to root-cause than it needed to be. Surfacing the stale-PID condition there (or in `codex doctor`) would help too, independent of the self-heal fix.

### What version of Codex CLI is running?

`gpt-6-astra` with reasoning effort set to `max`.

Native Windows 11 x64 (**not WSL**).

### What issue are you seeing?

When using GPT-6 Astra at `max` reasoning effort in Codex CLI on native Windows 11, the active Astra/TUI animation can trigger severe terminal rendering corruption instead of repainting cleanly in place.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/786102f3-d7e1-41b9-88d4-0be4645a3661

In the reproduced failure, the display repeatedly churns while Astra is active:

- large parts of the terminal are filled/repainted with dense dot/sparkle columns;
- stray ASCII letters appear across the redraw area;
- visible text degrades into repeated `?` glyphs;
- the composer / queued follow-up area becomes interleaved with the redraw;
- the apparent viewport keeps moving/churning instead of staying visually stable.

The model does not necessarily appear hard-crashed. The failure is primarily in the interactive terminal presentation while Astra is active, and it becomes especially disruptive during long `max` reasoning turns.

This is specifically a **native Windows + PowerShell** reproduction, not the WSL2 path described in #43369.

### Screen-recording evidence

A ~42 second H.264 screen recording of the reproduction was reviewed. It visibly shows the failure progressing from the Astra animation into terminal-wide redraw corruption. Near the end of the recording, the Codex status line visibly shows `gpt-6-astra max`.

The recording also shows the queued follow-up/composer content being visually mixed into the corrupted redraw region, so this appears broader than a cosmetic sparkle artifact.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Open Windows Terminal on Windows 11.
2. Start native Windows PowerShell 7 (not WSL).
3. Launch Codex CLI.
4. Select `gpt-6-astra`.
5. Set reasoning effort to `max`.
6. Start a task that causes Astra to remain active for an extended period.
7. Observe the Astra/TUI animation while the model is active.
8. The terminal begins repeatedly redrawing/churning instead of staying stable; in the captured reproduction this escalates into widespread dot/character corruption and affects the composer/queued-input area.

### What is the expected behavior?

Astra's decorative/thinking animation should update in place without corrupting other TUI regions, extending/churning the viewport, or damaging the readability of existing text and queued input.

Long `max` reasoning turns should remain visually stable in Windows Terminal.

### Additional information

This looks related to the broader Astra/TUI redraw family, but the closest existing reports I found use different environments or symptoms:

- #43369 — Windows 11 + Windows Terminal, but Codex CLI runs inside **WSL2** and the main symptom is terminal freezing/unresponsiveness.
- #44398 — Astra composer sparkle redraw problem on **macOS + kitty**.
- #45453 — Astra redraw interfering with selection/scrolling on **Linux + xfce-terminal**.
- #35654 — native Windows Terminal scroll/selection/copy problems during active rendering, but not specifically this Astra terminal-wide corruption.
- #44830 — native Windows Astra animation rendering artifacts, but centered on CLI pets/flashing blocks rather than composer/thinking redraw corruption.
- #42020 — native Windows inline-TUI scrollback loss in VS Code, potentially relevant to Windows inline rendering but a different visible failure.

Potential investigation lead: Astra's composer/whimsy animation performs periodic redraws. It may be worth checking whether repeated redraws on the native Windows terminal backend are invalidating too large a region, extending/reflowing inline scrollback, or failing to restore cells correctly.

A useful A/B test is:

```powershell
codex -c tui.whimsy=false
```

and, if needed:

```powershell
codex -c tui.animations=false -c tui.whimsy=false
```

I have not marked either workaround as confirmed yet.

## Why

Standalone web search selected a proxy route only for the initial endpoint. Redirect destinations can require a different system proxy route.

- Map route-aware failures to transport errors and remove request URLs from those errors.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for redirects through distinct proxies, preservation of POST bodies and default headers, URL authentication and header precedence, and transport error classification without URL leakage.

Injecting context before the first turn currently forces a full flush. Stores need a preparation checkpoint that can leave disposable context in memory, while local storage must keep prepared context durable before the first user input.

- Flush local storage at preparation checkpoints so injected context survives restart.

## Testing

Add tests showing that preparation and first sampling can proceed without waiting for durable metadata. Cover prepared context in first and follow-up requests, plus durability before first input and restoration after restart, in both legacy and paginated history modes.

items.body: ## Summary OpenAI's official desktop client (`ChatGPT Beta` / `OpenAI.CodexBeta`) is being systematically blocked by OpenAI's own Cloudflare WAF. While browser sessions ([chatgpt.com](https://chatgpt.com)) pass Turnstile challenges automatically, the desktop application's internal background daemon (`codex.exe`) is a native Rust HTTP client that cannot evaluate browser JavaScript. Cloudflare's bot management classifies direct API calls from this daemon as an automated scraping tool and blocks them with `HTTP 403 Forbidden` (Managed Challenge). As a result: 1. The daemon fails to fetch the user's subscription metadata from `auth.openai.com/api/accounts`. 2. The internal `account/read` RPC falls back to `planType: "unknown"`. 3. The Electron frontend UI misinterprets the account as belonging to an unauthorized enterprise workspace, completely hides all existing local chat history, and renders the generic modal: `"🔒 You don't have access to Codex yet. Contact your admin to request access."` This affects personal ChatGPT Plus subscribers who have no workspace administrators. ## Environment - **OS**: Windows 11 Core (Build 10.0.26220 x64) - **App Version**: `ChatGPT (Beta)` / `OpenAI.CodexBeta_26.727.4816.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0` - **Core Binary**: `codex.exe` (`0.146.0-alpha.9.2`) - **Subscription**: Personal ChatGPT Plus (`role: owner`, `is_default: true`, Personal Organization: `org-`) - **Web Browser Access**: Normal (chat history, Plus features, and models work as expected on Chrome/Brave) ## Technical Root Cause (Verified with Raw Telemetry) ### 1. Local Chat History is Intact in SQLite Querying the internal app-server daemon directly via JSON-RPC (`thread/list`) confirms that all local threads and session data in `~/.codex/state_5.sqlite` and `thread_history_1.sqlite` remain intact: ```json { "data": [ { "id": "01a0bf83-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx", "preview": "", "title": "" } ] } ``` The data is not lost. The frontend UI intentionally hides the sidebar because the user's account state cannot be verified. ### 2. Frontend Guards Block UI Due to `planType: "unknown"` Tracing the internal app-server communication (`account/read` RPC called by the Electron UI on launch) returns: ```json { "id": 3, "result": { "account": { "type": "chatgpt", "email": "", "planType": "unknown" }, "requiresOpenaiAuth": true } } ``` Because `planType` resolves to `"unknown"`, the UI executes its authorization guard: it suppresses the "Personal" workspace, disables chat history projection, and displays the fallback enterprise error modal. ### 3. Root Failure: Cloudflare Managed Challenge (403) Intercepts Backend Daemon Decompilation and runtime inspection of `codex.exe` reveals that the daemon queries personal subscription metadata via: - `https://auth.openai.com/api/accounts` - `https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/me` When `codex.exe` issues HTTP requests with a valid bearer token, Cloudflare WAF intercepts the traffic and responds with `HTTP 403 Forbidden` containing a Turnstile Managed Challenge HTML payload: ```text HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden CF-Ray: -KIX (Cloudflare Edge) Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8 Just a moment... Enable JavaScript and cookies to continue ``` Because `codex.exe` lacks a JavaScript runtime, it cannot satisfy the Turnstile challenge. Consequently: - `auth.tokens.account_id` is left empty (`""`). - `logs_2.sqlite` loops continuously: `waiting to resolve remote control preference until authentication is available error=remote control enrollment is waiting for a ChatGPT account id` - `account/read` returns `planType: "unknown"`. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. Install the ChatGPT Desktop App (`OpenAI.CodexBeta` or official Windows package). 2. Log in using a Personal ChatGPT Plus account. 3. Observe that all chat history is absent from the sidebar. 4. Attempt to access Codex; observe the modal: `"You don't have access to Codex yet. Contact your admin to request access."` 5.
